performers: Mary Garden, soprano; Claude Debussy, piano
intro: Mélisande sings this song at her tower window while combing her loosened hair. Mary Garden, the first Mélisande, recorded it with Debussy at the piano; after his prelude, the voice is unaccompanied for most of the song.

sections.label: A · Prelude and Mélisande’s song
sections.mNote: A piano prelude leads to unaccompanied singing.

sections.label: B · Three saints, Sunday noon
sections.mNote: The voice names three saints, then sings of a Sunday at noon.

cues.title: Mélisande at the tower window
cues.text: A piano prelude marked Doux et calme repeats its quavers beneath held notes. Mélisande appears at a window, combing her loosened hair. The piano stops when she sings, Modéré et librement, of her hair reaching down to the foot of the tower, and the vocal line moves through repeated notes.
cues.evidence: Debussy, Pelléas et Mélisande, Fromont vocal score (1902), plate E. 1416 F., Act III, scene 1, pp. 102–103: Doux et calme prelude, stage direction and unaccompanied Modéré et librement song. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/d/d6/IMSLP33280-PMLP09094-Debussy-L088vsFR.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mary Garden as Mélisande, 1902
cues.text: Mary Garden created the role of Mélisande in 1902, with André Messager conducting. Two years later, in Paris, she recorded this scene with Debussy.
cues.evidence: The Fromont vocal score’s original cast lists Mlle Garden as Mélisande and André Messager as conductor. The Record Collector’s IRCC discography, entry 106, identifies Garden and Debussy, Paris 1904. https://www.therecordcollector.org/articles/HRSandIRCCdiscographies/internationalrecordcollectorsclub.php

cues.title: Mélisande’s unaccompanied stanza
cues.text: After a two-bar piano link, Mélisande sings alone again. She names Daniel, Michael and Raphael, then says she was born on a Sunday at noon, and the line slows on those words, marked En retenant. The piano takes over where her song ends.
cues.evidence: Fromont vocal score, pp. 103–104: two-bar piano link, unaccompanied Saint Daniel et Saint Michel stanza, Sunday-birth lines, En retenant and instrumental continuation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Piano link between two stanzas
transitions.how: The piano enters beneath Mélisande’s held final word, jour. Low quavers move under sustained treble notes for two bars of 6/4, ending on a fermata. The voice then resumes unaccompanied in 4/4 with the stanza naming the saints.
transitions.evidence: Fromont vocal score, p. 103: piano entry overlapping jour, two-bar 6/4 interlude with fermata, and unaccompanied 4/4 second stanza.

source.title: Debussy, Pelléas et Mélisande · Fromont1902 vocal score, plateE.1416F.
source.locator: Act III, scene 1, printed pp. 102–104: piano prelude, two unaccompanied stanzas, a short piano link and the closing instrumental phrase.

timeline.note: Quiet piano quavers move beneath held treble notes.
Mélisande sings alone at the tower window.
The piano enters beneath the last held word, then continues alone.
The voice sings unaccompanied; the text names the saints and a birth on a Sunday.
After the voice stops, the piano plays a quiet closing phrase.

composer.epithet: Composer who trusted his ear over the rules (“pleasure is the law”) and wrote new sounds for the piano, the flute and the orchestra.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and was imprisoned for it. In prison he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on as a pupil. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, described him in January 1874 as “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament”; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Around 1890, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud, he said: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
